title: The Expressivity Boundary of Probabilistic Circuits: A Comparison with Large Language Models
claim: Replacing probability-space convex-combination outputs with logit-space projections consistently lowers loss at the same latent size, across model families and datasets.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row, shared legend on top, loss vs latent size
description: A single row of three line charts with one shared legend above. The legend names four series: Logit-HMM (blue), HMM (gray-green), Transformer (purple) and Prob-Transformer (red). Each panel plots validation loss on the y-axis against latent size d on the x-axis, one panel per dataset: (a) Simple Word with |V|=54 and d from 4 to 10, (b) PTB with |V|=50257 and d from 8 to 128, and (c) WikiText with |V|=50257 and d from 8 to 128. All curves fall as d grows. In every panel the logit-space models (Logit-HMM, Transformer) sit below their probability-space counterparts (HMM, Prob-Transformer). The gap is large at small d, and in PTB the HMM and Prob-Transformer curves nearly converge at large d. The eye goes first to the gap between the gray-green HMM line at the top and the lower purple and blue lines.
caption: Impact of output parameterization on modeling performance. Lower validation loss is better. Across all datasets, logit-space variants improve over their probability-space counterparts within the same model family: Logit-HMM improves over HMM, and Transformer improves over Prob-Transformer. This supports the hypothesis that probability-space convex combinations impose a stronger geometric constraint than logit-space projections under a limited latent dimension.
abstract: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are deep generative models that support exact and efficient probabilistic inference. Yet in autoregressive language modeling, PCs still lag behind Transformer-based large language models (LLMs), suggesting an important expressivity gap. In this work, we compare PCs and LLMs under a unified autoregressive formulation. First, an output bottleneck: PCs parameterize predictions as convex combinations in probability space, which struggles to represent the sharp distributions typical of language; adopting a logit-space parameterization substantially narrows this gap. Second, a context-encoding bottleneck: we prove that structured-decomposable PCs can match Transformer separation rank on vtree-aligned partitions, but show, both theoretically and empirically, that this capacity is limited to partitions aligned with the fixed routing structure, leading to severe degradation when the data exhibits heterogeneous dependency topologies. We further prove that decomposable PCs are strictly more expressive than structured-decomposable ones, though effectively optimizing them remains an open challenge.
